findings.claim: Not hollandaise, which is lemon and butter only.
findings.because: Hollandaise is built on egg yolks just as bearnaise is. Saying it is 'lemon and butter only' teaches a server that one of the two sauces has no yolk, and that is exactly the wrong thing to repeat to a guest who is avoiding egg.
findings.fix: Not hollandaise, the same yolks and butter with lemon. This one is flecked green with tarragon.

findings.claim: Airy froth whipped up with a hand blender to top a plate
findings.because: On modern menus an 'emulsion' (brown butter, dashi-butter, beurre blanc style) is very often frothed with a hand blender just before plating and served airy. So this trap can be true of the menu word, and its why ('it is creamy, not airy') is not reliably true.
findings.fix: says: "Clear broth set firm with gelatin and sliced cold"; why: "That is an aspic; this is fat and water held as droplets, not a set gel."

findings.claim: Fat and water held together as tiny droplets in one smooth sauce
findings.because: This literally describes hollandaise, aioli and vinaigrette too. Shown as a distractor under any of those terms it is a true answer, and under Emulsion any of their gists would pass. The gist needs to mark this card as the kitchen word for the state, not as a particular sauce.
findings.fix: Kitchen word for oil and water beaten into one stable mix

findings.claim: Not hollandaise, which is lemon and butter only.
findings.because: Hollandaise is egg yolk, butter and lemon. Saying 'lemon and butter only' tells a new hire it has no egg, and they may repeat that to a guest who asks about egg.
findings.fix: Not hollandaise, which has lemon, not herbs.

findings.claim: Light sauce made only for beef, like the dip served with a French dip
findings.because: 'the dip served with a French dip' repeats itself and reads badly as an answer option. A cleaner version keeps the required beef mistake and the same length band.
findings.fix: Light sauce used only for beef, the dip for a French dip sandwich

findings.claim: which matters to a guest asking about lightly cooked egg.
findings.because: This says the fact matters but never tells the server what to do with it. A third-day hire needs the action: send the question to the kitchen.
findings.fix: The yolks are warmed, not cooked firm: send undercooked egg questions to the kitchen.

findings.claim: Not gravy, which is thickened with flour
findings.because: Set against gravy, this tells a server that jus has no flour, which a guest avoiding wheat would take as an assurance. Many kitchens finish a jus lié with starch, and some use a little roux or flour-dusted meat. The card's own why says it is 'only lightly thickened'. The real difference is how thick it is, not whether flour is used.
findings.fix: Not gravy, which is thickened much further, and not demi-glace, a far thicker veal reduction.

findings.claim: Held warm, never hot: too much heat scrambles the yolks and the sauce splits.
findings.because: The note leaves out the fact a server most needs: the egg yolks are only gently warmed and never set firm, so this is lightly cooked egg, just as on the hollandaise card. A guest who asks about undercooked egg deserves a plain answer that sends them to the kitchen about pasteurized eggs.
findings.fix: The yolks are only gently warmed, never set firm; ask the kitchen whether its eggs are pasteurized.

findings.claim: which matters to a guest asking about lightly cooked egg
findings.because: The note hints at a concern but gives the server nothing to do about it. The plain fact is that the yolks stay lightly cooked, and the question to take back to the kitchen is whether it uses pasteurized eggs, as the aioli card already says.
findings.fix: The yolks are only gently warmed, never set firm. Ask the kitchen whether it uses pasteurized eggs.

findings.claim: "oil"
findings.because: Vinaigrettes are often made with walnut or hazelnut oil, and a guest with a tree-nut allergy needs that flagged by name. Plain 'oil' hides it.
findings.fix: "oil", "sometimes walnut or hazelnut oil"

findings.claim: sometimes anchovy
findings.because: The classic French remoulade (Escoffier) is mayonnaise with mustard, gherkins, capers, herbs and anchovy essence. Anchovy belongs to the classic recipe, not an occasional extra, and a guest with a fish allergy needs it flagged at that strength.
findings.fix: often anchovy

findings.claim: It starts with mayonnaise, an emulsion of egg yolk and oil
findings.because: The old-line New Orleans red remoulade (Arnaud's, Galatoire's style) is often oil-based, like a vinaigrette, with no mayonnaise at all. The card calls mayonnaise universal and then describes the Louisiana version as a variant of it.
findings.fix: Most start with mayonnaise, an emulsion of egg yolk and oil

findings.claim: dansk-remoulade
findings.because: Danish remoulade is a different, yellow sauce colored with curry or turmeric and served with fried fish and hot dogs. The card describes only the French and Louisiana versions, so a server who follows the link gets a sauce the card never mentions.
findings.fix: omit recipe

findings.claim: often red wine
findings.because: The classic demi-glace (Escoffier) is espagnole and brown stock reduced together and finished with Madeira or sometimes sherry, not red wine. Red wine belongs to its child sauces, such as bordelaise.
findings.fix: often madeira

findings.claim: Too hot or too cold and it splits into oil
findings.because: Heat is what breaks it into oil. When it gets too cold the butter sets solid, and the sauce only breaks once it is warmed again. The card should not tell servers that cold alone turns it into oil.
findings.fix: Too hot and it splits into oil, too cold and it sets

findings.claim: It's a deeply reduced veal sauce
findings.because: Veal is the classic base, but many American kitchens make demi-glace from beef or chicken bones, or buy a base. A server who repeats this line tells a guest who avoids veal what the plate holds, and it may not be true of this kitchen. The why and madeWith already say 'traditionally veal', so the guest line should hedge the same way.
findings.fix: It's a deeply reduced meat sauce, classically veal

findings.claim: It's what makes a lasagna, a gratin or a croque monsieur so rich.
findings.because: Most American lasagna is layered with ricotta, not béchamel. The béchamel version is the Bolognese style. A new hire at an Italian-American place who says this about the house lasagna will be wrong.
findings.fix: It's what makes a classic lasagna, a gratin or a croque monsieur so rich.

findings.claim: a rich broth clarified until it is perfectly clear
findings.because: 'Clarified until clear' says the same thing twice and uses a kitchen word without explaining it. A guest who asks 'what is that?' learns nothing about how it gets clear. Egg white is the plain answer, and it is the fact the guest is most likely to ask about next.
findings.fix: a rich broth cleared with egg white until it is perfectly clear

findings.claim: It starts with mayonnaise, an emulsion of egg yolk and oil
findings.because: The card never says the base is uncooked. Kitchens that make their own mayonnaise usually whisk it from raw egg yolk, and commercial mayonnaise uses pasteurized egg. A guest who avoids raw egg will ask, and the server needs to know to check with the kitchen. The card has no note, so adding one does not repeat anything.
findings.fix: House-made versions are often whisked from raw egg yolk. Ask the kitchen whether theirs uses pasteurized egg.

findings.claim: "fruit or vegetable", "often sugar", "often lemon juice"
findings.because: Classic fruit coulis, especially raspberry, is often sharpened with a splash of liqueur such as kirsch or framboise, and it is served raw or barely cooked, so the alcohol stays in. madeWith should flag alcohol for guests who avoid it.
findings.fix: "fruit or vegetable", "often sugar", "often lemon juice", "sometimes liqueur"

findings.claim: a Catalan sauce of roasted red peppers and tomato
findings.because: The classic base is dried sweet peppers (ñora), soaked and ground, with roasted tomato and garlic. Roasted fresh bell peppers are a common American shortcut, and saying so contradicts the card's own gist and why.
findings.fix: a Catalan sauce of dried sweet red peppers and roasted tomato

findings.claim: It is cooked and ground smooth, built on roasted peppers, nuts and bread.
findings.because: The sauce itself is not cooked: its tomato and garlic are roasted, its peppers are dried and soaked, and the whole is pounded or ground raw. Traditional romesco is also coarse and rustic, not smooth.
findings.fix: It is ground from dried peppers, roasted tomato, nuts and bread, not chopped raw.

findings.claim: first made by fishermen for their catch
findings.because: The Tarragona fishermen story (Serrallo quarter) is a local tradition, not a documented fact. A server will repeat it as a fact.
findings.fix: said to come from its fishermen

findings.claim: simmer gently in water for hours
findings.because: This holds for chicken and veal. Fish stock (fumet) and shellfish stock, both in this card's madeWith, simmer only about 20 to 45 minutes, because longer cooking turns them bitter and chalky.
findings.fix: simmer gently in water, for hours, or under an hour for fish

findings.claim: "sometimes fish bones", "sometimes shellfish shells"
findings.because: Fish fumet is classically made with white wine, and brown stock with tomato paste. Alcohol is one of the flags this section asks for, and it is missing.
findings.fix: replace "sometimes shellfish shells" with "sometimes white wine" or merge fish and shellfish into one item and add "sometimes white wine"

findings.claim: It is served cold, never cooked.
findings.because: Italian salsa verde is served at room temperature, never chilled. A server who calls it cold misleads the guest.
findings.fix: It is served at room temperature, never cooked.

findings.claim: "sometimes bread"
findings.because: Many Piedmontese versions (bagnet verd) also use hard-boiled egg. Egg is a flag a guest with an allergy would need.
findings.fix: replace "garlic" or merge so the list gets "sometimes hard-boiled egg" alongside "sometimes bread"

findings.claim: bones and vegetables simmered for hours into a rich liquid. It's what gives our sauces
findings.because: The card's own madeWith lists fish bones and shellfish shells, and fish stock is simmered only about 20 to 30 minutes; 'for hours' is false for those. 'Our sauces' also has the server assert this kitchen's practice, which the card cannot know.
findings.fix: bones and vegetables simmered slowly in water. It's what gives sauces

findings.claim: Spring pea soup, chicken stock, mint, crème fraîche
findings.because: Menus almost never list stock as a component of a soup, because it is already in the soup base, so this does not read like a real menu. Stock shows up on a menu when a dish is steamed or finished in it.
findings.fix: Steamed clams, fish stock, white wine, grilled bread

findings.claim: pounded with pine nuts, garlic, Parmesan and olive oil
findings.because: Most restaurant pesto is made in a blender or food processor. A server who tells a guest it is pounded is making a claim the kitchen may not back up. The why already covers what the name means.
findings.fix: made with pine nuts, garlic, Parmesan and olive oil

findings.claim: roasted red peppers and tomato
findings.because: The why says the classic sauce uses dried sweet peppers that are soaked, with the tomato roasted, so the guest line and the why disagree. A server who reads both will not know which one to repeat.
findings.fix: sweet dried red peppers and roasted tomato

findings.claim: SAHL-sah VEHR-deh
findings.because: This is the Italian ending. An American dining room says the final syllable as 'day', as in the familiar Mexican salsa verde, and the key has 'ay' for that sound.
findings.fix: SAHL-sah VEHR-day

findings.claim: ah-groh-DOHL-cheh
findings.because: This is the native Italian ending. American servers and guests say the last syllable as 'chay', and the key has 'ay' for that sound.
findings.fix: ah-groh-DOHL-chay

findings.claim: "parsley", "olive oil", "capers", "often anchovy", "garlic", "vinegar", "sometimes bread"
findings.because: The card's origin points to Piedmont, and the Piedmontese version (bagnet verd) is often made with hard-boiled egg or egg yolk. Many Italian recipes add it too. Egg is a major allergen, and this list never mentions it. The list is already at its limit of 7, but vinegar is covered in both the gist and the why, so it can come out to make room.
findings.fix: "parsley", "olive oil", "capers", "often anchovy", "garlic", "sometimes bread", "sometimes hard-boiled egg"

findings.claim: Kitchens leave it unsalted on purpose, because it gets reduced into sauces and the salt would concentrate.
findings.because: This states that every kitchen's stock is unsalted. A guest limiting sodium could take that as a promise. Many kitchens salt stock lightly, and bought-in bases are often salted. The accurate claim is that it is usually left unsalted.
findings.fix: Kitchens usually leave it unsalted, because it gets reduced into sauces and salt would concentrate.

critic.notes: Coverage and the rules I checked. All 21 roster rows have a card. Section mean is 667 chars (ceiling 720); the longest card is fd_0209 at 779 and none is over 900. No verdict words, em or en dashes, or banned substrings (scanned mechanically). Every accented term has a say. The Jus knownPacketError is covered: its trap says 'used only for beef'. No two gists or guest lines are duplicates. Velouté/Béchamel and Chimichurri/Salsa Verde have parallel gists but each names what sets it apart. Confusion pairs Hollandaise/Béarnaise, Hollandaise/Beurre Blanc, Jus/Demi-Glace and Gastrique/Agrodolce are linked both ways. Consommé->Stock and Coulis->Compote are one-way, which is acceptable. Optional ideas: add 'Brown Butter' (fd_0161) to seeAlsoTerms on Beurre Blanc, since guests mix up the beurre sauces. The Agrodolce gist lists raisins and onion as if they were fixed, though the why says 'often'; 'Italian sweet-sour sauce of vinegar and sugar, often with raisins' would be more accurate if it fits the length. Agrodolce notThis (132) and Demi-Glace guest (158) are over their aim ranges but inside the limits.
